sections.title: Azure portal: web-based management
points: The Azure portal is a browser-based console at portal.azure.com for creating and managing all your Azure resources in one place.
Because it runs in a browser, it works on any OS and device: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android. Nothing has to be installed.
It needs an internet connection and a sign-in. Command-line management is a separate option (Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Cloud Shell).
From a phone or tablet, use the Azure portal or Cloud Shell; locally installed tools (Windows PowerShell, Azure Storage Explorer) are not the answer for mobile.
Cloud services and other resources can be managed from the portal, the command line, or APIs; management is not limited to Windows devices.

sections.title: Marketplace and portal blades
points: Azure Marketplace: catalog to find, try, and buy Microsoft and third-party solutions, such as VM images and security appliances, to deploy to a subscription.
Microsoft Store is for consumer/Microsoft products, not Azure deployments; a subscription is a billing and access boundary, not a store.
Monitor blade: monitor health and performance of services and resources.
Advisor blade: personalized recommendations, including security; Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the dedicated security posture service.

sections.title: Azure Cloud Shell
points: Cloud Shell is an authenticated, browser-accessible shell for managing Azure. Nothing needs to be installed locally.
Start it from a web browser: the Azure portal toolbar or shell.azure.com. It works from any OS, including Android tablets and Chrome OS.
You choose Bash or PowerShell as the experience. Azure CLI (az) commands run in both.
To create a VM from an Android tablet: the Azure portal, Cloud Shell (Bash), or Cloud Shell (PowerShell). The PowerApps portal does not manage Azure VMs.
Azure CLI is not installed by default on Windows 11; Cloud Shell has it preinstalled.

sections.title: Azure CLI: where it runs
points: Azure CLI (az commands) is cross-platform: install it on Windows, macOS, or Linux.
On Windows you can run az from Command Prompt or Windows PowerShell (or Windows Terminal). Tools like Firewall or Network and Sharing Center are unrelated.
Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell both run on Windows, Linux, and macOS; the Azure portal works in any browser.
So a Windows 10, Ubuntu, or macOS computer can use the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and the portal.

sections.title: Azure PowerShell: running PowerShell scripts
points: Azure PowerShell (the Az module) manages Azure with PowerShell cmdlets and is cross-platform: Windows, macOS, and Linux.
To run a PowerShell script that creates resources you need PowerShell with the Az module installed, or Cloud Shell (PowerShell) from a browser.
Having only Azure CLI tools installed does not let you run PowerShell scripts; CLI uses az commands.
The Az module needs a supported PowerShell version (Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7.x). Old PowerShell Core 6.0 is out of support.
Valid hosts: Windows with the Az module, Chrome OS using Cloud Shell, or macOS/Linux with a supported PowerShell and Az.

sections.title: Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources
points: Azure Arc extends Azure Resource Manager to resources outside Azure: you project them into Azure and manage them like Azure resources.
On-premises Windows Server and Linux servers (physical or virtual) can be managed from the Azure portal by connecting them to Arc.
Azure Arc is the answer for a unified way to project and manage non-Azure resources in ARM.
Not Arc: Azure AD Connect syncs identities; Azure Migrate assesses and moves workloads; Front Door is a web traffic service; AKS runs Kubernetes in Azure.

sections.title: Arc for hybrid and multicloud governance
points: Arc supports servers, Kubernetes clusters, and data services (SQL Server, PostgreSQL) hosted on-premises, at the edge, or in other clouds.
It applies Azure management and governance (Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, RBAC) consistently across hybrid and multicloud environments.
Arc-enabled Kubernetes can manage clusters at scale, and third-party or non-Azure databases can be managed as Arc-enabled data services.
Azure Policy defines rules; Arc is what extends compliance and monitoring reach to resources outside Azure.

sections.title: Azure DevTest Labs
points: DevTest Labs lets teams quickly create and remove environments (VMs) from ARM templates, with policies, quotas, and auto-shutdown to control cost.
It minimizes admin effort for developers who repeatedly deploy and delete many VMs.
Scale sets: autoscale identical VMs. Reserved VM Instances: discounted committed-use pricing. Azure Virtual Desktop: hosted desktops.

sections.title: Azure DevOps services: Repos
points: Azure DevOps is a set of development services: Repos, Pipelines, Boards, Test Plans, and Artifacts.
Azure Repos: Git (and TFVC) version control tools to manage code.
Azure Pipelines: CI/CD builds and deployments. Azure Boards: work tracking.
Infrastructure as code (templates, scripts) is stored and versioned in source control such as Repos.

sections.title: ARM templates: repeatable deployments
points: ARM templates are declarative JSON files that define infrastructure; this is infrastructure as code.
One template can define many resources and be deployed repeatedly with the same result, so each resource does not need its own template.
Deploy templates through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or REST API.
For identical resources across business units, use ARM templates. Management groups organize subscriptions; API Management publishes APIs; scale sets scale VMs.
Resource groups are logical containers; Azure Policy enforces rules on what can be deployed. Neither deploys resources from a definition.

sections.title: ARM as the management layer and APIs
points: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management service for Azure. Every tool (portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs) calls the ARM REST APIs.
A desktop application interacts with Azure and manages resources by calling APIs (REST/SDKs).
Templates describe what to deploy; CLI and Cloud Shell are tools that call the APIs.

sections.title: What Azure Advisor does
points: Advisor is a free personalized cloud consultant: it analyzes your resource configuration and usage and recommends best practices.
Recommendation categories: Reliability, Security, Operational excellence, Performance, and Cost.
It covers resources across multiple subscriptions and can alert you to new recommendations.
It does not estimate costs of a planned solution (pricing calculator), assess on-premises migration (Azure Migrate), or integrate AD (Azure AD Connect).
Advisor does not list backed-up VMs, configure VM network settings, or set a deadline for acting; acting on security advice improves your secure score.

sections.title: Advisor cost recommendations
points: Advisor identifies underutilized or idle resources, such as VMs with low CPU use, and suggests resizing, shutting down, or buying reservations.
Use Advisor to get recommendations that reduce Azure costs.
Cost Management + Billing analyzes spending and budgets. The pricing calculator estimates new deployments. Reservations are a discount, not an analyzer.
Service Health reports Azure incidents, not savings.

sections.title: Advisor versus related services
points: Azure Advisor: recommendations to improve an environment. Azure Monitor: health and performance data. Application Insights: monitors web apps.
Azure DevOps: integrated code deployment and planning. Azure Cognitive Services (AI services): prebuilt AI APIs.
In the portal, use the Advisor blade for security recommendations and the Monitor blade for health of services.

sections.title: Azure Service Health scope
points: Azure Service Health gives a personalized view of the health of the Azure services, regions, and resources you use.
It covers service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories, and sits alongside Azure status (global) and Resource health (individual resources).
You can create service health alerts to be notified of incidents and planned maintenance.
It reports and notifies; it cannot prevent a service failure.
Azure Advisor gives recommendations; Azure Monitor gives telemetry; neither is the planned maintenance notification service.

sections.title: Finding health notifications in the portal
points: In the portal, Service Health is reached from Help + support and from Azure Monitor.
Use it to view planned maintenance events and service failure notifications that can affect your subscription.
For a VM in a region, check Service Health (under Monitor) for outages in that region and service.

sections.title: Azure Monitor as the central data platform
points: Azure Monitor collects, analyzes, and acts on telemetry from Azure, on-premises, and other clouds, across multiple subscriptions.
Monitor data (metrics and logs) is stored; log data goes to a Log Analytics workspace.
Log Analytics is the tool where you run Kusto (KQL) queries to compare events across many resources.
Azure AD activity logs can be routed to Azure Monitor. Azure Monitor integrates with Application Insights and Log Analytics.
Event Hubs streams events, Stream Analytics processes streams, Service Health is health reporting; they are not the monitoring repository.

sections.title: Azure Monitor alerts
points: Alerts notify you or run automation when a condition is met on metrics, logs (including Log Analytics workspace data), or activity log events.
For example, an activity log alert can fire when an administrator stops a VM.
Alerts use action groups to send notifications such as email, SMS, voice, or push and to trigger webhooks, runbooks, and Logic Apps.
Azure Monitor can monitor on-premises computers, not only Azure VMs.

sections.title: Application Insights
points: Application Insights is an Azure Monitor feature for application performance management.
Use it for web apps: page load times in the browser, request rates, response times, failures, and dependencies.
Log Analytics queries log data, Network Watcher diagnoses networks, and alerts only notify.

sections.title: Activity log: who did what
points: The Azure activity log records subscription-level events: who did what, and when, for write operations such as stopping a VM.
Use it to find which user turned off a VM; it keeps data for a limited time (90 days by default).

sections.title: What an SLA guarantees
points: An Azure SLA is a formal Microsoft commitment to performance standards, mainly uptime (availability), not features, bandwidth, or performance.
Monthly uptime % = (Maximum Available Minutes - Downtime Minutes) / Maximum Available Minutes x 100.
If the SLA is not met, you receive service credits for that service against your bill, not a refund of other services.
Azure SLAs vary by service and configuration; most paid services start at 99.9%. Microsoft Entra ID Premium P2 is covered at 99.9%, whereas Free has no SLA.
Services in preview are excluded from SLAs.

sections.title: Composite SLAs
points: A composite SLA covers an application that depends on multiple services. Multiply the individual SLAs together.
Do not use the minimum, maximum, or divide. Chaining dependencies lowers the composite.
Redundant paths (for example, resources in multiple regions) can raise the effective SLA.

sections.title: Raising availability for a VM workload
points: VM SLAs rise with redundancy: a single VM with premium storage 99.9%, availability sets 99.95%, two or more VMs across availability zones 99.99%.
To reach 99.99%, deploy at least two VMs spread across two or more availability zones; one zone or one VM is not enough.
Deploying to multiple regions can increase guaranteed uptime; buying multiple subscriptions does not.

sections.title: Private preview, public preview, GA
points: Typical lifecycle: private preview, public preview, general availability (GA).
Private preview: invitation only for selected customers. Public preview: available to any customer with an Azure subscription. GA: released to all customers.
Preview services are visible in the regular portal and can be managed with portal, CLI, and PowerShell; the portal labels previews.
Preview pricing is often discounted; GA is billed at normal rates, so the price does not drop at GA.
After GA, services continue to receive new features, and existing preview resources generally need not be recreated.

sections.title: Preview terms: SLA and support
points: Public preview services are excluded from SLAs; each preview defines its own terms and support.
There is no standard SLA percentage for previews.
Previews can technically be used in production but this is not recommended, because there is no SLA guarantee.
Private previews do not require a separate portal.

sections.title: Modern Lifecycle Policy
points: The Modern Lifecycle Policy applies to continuously serviced products and services.
If there is no successor, Microsoft gives at least 12 months' notice before ending support (excluding free services and previews).
There is no fixed five-year mainstream support term under this policy (that is the Fixed Policy).

sections.title: Support plan tiers
points: Basic: included with all subscriptions; 24/7 billing and subscription support, docs, forums, Advisor, and Service Health.
Developer: business-hours technical support by email. Standard: 24/7 technical support by phone and email.
Professional Direct: Standard-level support plus architectural guidance. Premier: highest tier for enterprise customers with an Enterprise Agreement.
An Azure free account has the Basic plan. Community forums are open to everyone, not only pay-as-you-go.
Support requests can be opened under every plan, including Basic (nontechnical for Basic); the plan decides the support type and response.

sections.title: Phone and email access to engineers
points: Basic has no technical support. Developer has email only, during business hours.
Standard, Professional Direct, and Premier include phone and email access to support engineers 24/7.
The lowest-cost plan with 24/7 phone access to engineers is Standard.

sections.title: Architectural guidance
points: Professional Direct includes architecture support and guidance on workload design.
It is the lowest-cost plan offering this; Premier costs more, and Standard/Developer lack it.

sections.title: Opening requests and quota increases
points: Create a support request in the Azure portal, from Help + support, or from a resource's Support + troubleshooting menu.
Quota increases are also requested via Help + support (new support request, quota issue type).
support.microsoft.com is not where Azure support requests are created.

sections.title: Azure Germany
points: Azure Germany was a separate sovereign instance of Azure in German datacenters for data residency.
It was available to eligible customers and partners globally, not only German residents or German-registered enterprises.
The service has been retired in favor of Azure regions in Germany.

sections.title: Azure Blueprints
points: A blueprint packages artifacts into a repeatable definition: ARM templates, Azure Policy assignments, role assignments (RBAC), and resource groups.
You assign a blueprint to a subscription, not to a resource group.
Blueprint resource locks (Read Only or Do Not Delete) are enforced by the assignment and re-applied, even if someone removes the lock manually.
Azure Blueprints (Preview) is scheduled to be retired on January 31, 2027.
